description_full: Gold.com, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, operates as a precious metals company. It operates through three segments: Wholesale Sales & Ancillary Services, Direct-to-Consumer, and Secured Lending. The Wholesale Sales & Ancillary Services segment sells gold, silver, platinum, and palladium in the form of bars, plates, powders, wafers, grains, ingots, and coins under the A-Mark brand. This segment also offers complementary services, such as receiving, handling, inventorying, processing, packing, and shipping of precious metals and custom coins on a secure basis; and designs and produces minted silver products. The Direct-to-Consumer segment sells and delivers gold, silver, platinum, palladium, and copper products directly to customers and the investor community through television, radio, and the internet, as well as through customer service outreach; rarities and numismatic collections; and numismatic and bullion products. It operates various websites targeting specific niches within the precious metals retail market. The Secured Lending segment originates and acquires commercial loans secured by bullion, numismatic coins, and graded sports cards. The company serves customers, including financial institutions, bullion retailers, industrial manufacturers and fabricators, sovereign mints, refiners, coin and metal dealers, investors, collectors, and e-commerce and other retail customers. It operates in the United States, Europe, Canada, the Asia Pacific, Africa, Australia, and South America. The company was formerly known as A-Mark Precious Metals, Inc. and changed its name to Gold.com, Inc. in December 2025. The company was founded in 1965 and is headquartered in Costa Mesa, California.

financial_summary: Gold.com, Inc. is a small-cap financial services business with a $1.1B market cap on $25.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +40% over the past three years and +14% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.

Returns on capital run at 18% against a 10% cost of capital, a 8-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, and 1% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $1.2B in free cash flow — roughly 5 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 14.85× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -27.6% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.0× net debt/EBITDA, and thin 2.8× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Net dilution runs at 10.7% annually, transferring value from owners to stock-based comp, and insiders hold 34% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and profit capture is only 0.0× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.
